copy_pick.why: Candidate 2's blurb 'BAHRAIN RADAR SITE, INTERCEPTORS FIRING' is clipped field-note form, and its summary avoids yesterday's 'less a X than a Y' shape and the recent 'at least something' closer that Candidates 1 and 3 reuse, ending instead on a fresher line about the planet still dropping things.

doom.driver: Iran says it targets US radar in Bahrain. What do we know?.
doom.summary: Iran says it went after a US radar in Bahrain, Ukraine has quietly taken a third of Russia's refineries offline, and Sudan is being switched off one power station at a time. Back home, America grounded every plane because someone fiddled with a router, which is less comforting than a cyberattack, not more. SpaceX catching a Starship with chopsticks is lovely, but the planet down here is still dropping things.

factors.detail: Open-model quantizations and an AI heart-risk detector add up to steady progress, not a jump.

factors.detail: Iranian strikes on a US radar in Bahrain, Ukraine's refinery blitz and drone war in Sudan make for active multi-front conflict.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: A router-induced national ground stop, a defused bomb at an ethanol plant and a capsized cruise ship made for a clumsy, jumpy Saturday.

doom.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. A pre-dawn view over Bahrain's flat sand-colored coast near Riffa, the whole scene swallowed by a thick blood-red and furnace-orange dust haze that hangs in heavy layers and turns the sky into a glowing wall of fire-colored fog. Hellish orange glare rises from below, from burning-bright floodlights and a molten glow on the horizon, lighting the underside of the haze and every object in plain view, with shadows in bruised violet and deep maroon, never black. In the middle distance, inside a fenced, sandbagged compound of low tan buildings and a few palms, a large tilted flat-faced phased-array radar stands intact on a pedestal, its pale panel lit orange from below, with generators and cable runs around it. Beside it, a Patriot launcher with angled boxes points up into the haze. A line of small dark arrowhead-shaped delta-wing drones with tiny glowing exhaust points descends through the fog toward the radar, only partly clear of the murk, and bright interceptor streaks curve up to meet them as thin glowing trails. In the foreground, a rooftop siren pole on a flat-roofed building and a slim minaret with a lit green band rise into the haze, with a short chain-link fence in the lower corner. Far behind them, the glittering lights of Manama's towers glow as faint smeared orange blocks in the haze. The mood is malevolent, with nothing safe in the frame, and every part of the scene is bright and readable at small size.

minor: The radar panel is a flat, nearly featureless glowing slab, so it reads more like a billboard than a phased-array radar.
The Patriot launcher is partly fused with the truck and cable clutter, and its boxes are a bit muddled.
The interceptor streaks mostly stop at glowing orbs instead of clearly reaching the drones. Several of them cross the sky at inconsistent angles.
The drones are fairly large and clear rather than partly hidden in the haze, and they look like jets.
The minaret's top finial and its green-lit band are slightly smudged.
The siren pole has loudspeakers stacked in a slightly odd arrangement.
The chain-link fence in the lower right is a blurry texture.
The compound walls and sandbags are a repetitive brown blur at phone size.

dawn.driver: SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first. Starship Test Flight 15 marked the first time Elon Musk's company tried to catch both the booster and upper stage of the rocket.
dawn.summary: Two mechanical arms reached out from a Texas launch tower and caught Starship's upper stage as it lowered itself home, a first in spaceflight and a big step toward rockets that fly again and again. Outside Dallas, longtime custodian Marilyn Hampton was surprised with an elementary school bearing her name. In Bangkok, 19-year-old Carmelle carried the Philippines to victory at the first-ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

factors.name: Science
factors.detail: Astronomers spotted 2026 ED138, a large icy world beyond Pluto that could become the solar system's sixth recognized dwarf planet.

factors.name: Cooperation
factors.detail: Eurovision staged its first regional edition outside Europe, with Asian nations sharing one stage in Bangkok.

factors.name: Human Spirit
factors.detail: An Aubrey, Texas school district honored beloved custodian Marilyn Hampton by naming a new elementary school after her.

factors.name: Environment
factors.detail: Scientists found a simple way to turn used coffee grounds into biodiesel, and the leftover material can still feed other renewable fuels.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: Researchers in China named a new giant fungus, Dianjunus rex, which grows up to 20 inches tall.

dawn.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. EXTREME CLOSE-UP filling the entire frame on a symbolic metaphor: two enormous burnished-steel mechanical gripping arms, shown only as the inner curves of their steel pads, closing gently around a single glowing ember-orange sphere of warm light, like a returning homecoming star cradled in an open pair of hands made of machinery. The environment is implied only through the metal's reflections and the frame edges. The polished steel surfaces mirror a clean Texas Gulf coast morning: a flat green marsh-grass horizon, a thin pale sliver of tidal water, and a lattice tower silhouette stretching up through the reflection. Soft amber sunrise light pours across the steel from the left, lifting the shadows so that the deep crevices between the arm plates turn from murky olive to clear, readable sage green. The sphere is made of stainless-steel tile pixels, with a faint scorched-gold edge of reentry warmth on its underside and a tiny curved reflection of the Earth's blue limb. A single thin line of tiny white-gold pixel lights arcs across the top of the sphere like a delicate orbit necklace. In the lower corner of the arm's polished surface, a minuscule reflected crowd of whole, tiny silhouetted figures stands with raised arms. The palette is warm amber, honey gold, soft moss and sage green, and burnished silver, with crisp pixel dithering on the metal gradients, calm and triumphant, clarity arriving.

minor: The tiny reflected crowd in the lower-right steel pad is made of small silhouettes with raised arms. They are very small and read as a distant crowd, so they are acceptable.
The sphere's tile pattern warps unevenly and its orbit-necklace line of lights is slightly irregular. This fits the style.
The surrounding steel plates are hard to read as 'gripping arms'. They look more like petal or pod shapes, but this is a stylistic ambiguity and not a broken object.
The lattice tower is repeated in three of the reflections. This is plausible for mirrored surfaces.
